guidance: An estimate of mean wind speed at another height, not a wind resource assessment: it assumes flat open terrain, neutral stability and a long upwind fetch, and it does not model turbines, gusts, buildings, forest edges or complex terrain.
method: The page estimates the mean wind speed at a target height from a reading at another height using one of two neutral-atmosphere models. The power law multiplies the measured speed by the target height over the measurement height raised to an empirical exponent: about 0.143 (one seventh) over open land, 0.11 over open water and 0.2 to 0.4 over rough or built-up ground. The log law multiplies the measured speed by the logarithm of the target height over the roughness length, divided by the logarithm of the measurement height over the same roughness length, and the terrain menu carries the published roughness lengths: 0.0002 m for open sea, 0.005 m for mud flats or snow, 0.03 m for open flat grass, 0.1 m for low crops, 0.25 m for high crops, 0.5 m for parkland and bushes, 1 m for suburbs and forest and 2 m for a city centre. Because the log profile has no meaning close to the roughness elements, both heights must be at least ten times the roughness length; shorter masts over a city are refused rather than answered. The page also reports the speed ratio to the measurement, the height ratio and the wind-power ratio, which is the cube of the speed ratio because the power in a moving air stream grows with the cube of its speed. That ratio is not a turbine's output: a machine's power curve, cut-in and cut-out speeds, air density, availability and wake losses all matter. Both models assume flat ground with a long fetch upwind in neutral weather, so a ridge, building, forest edge or valley, and stable night air or gusts, can move the answer by more than the difference between the two laws. Everything runs in your browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Wind profile power law: u/ur = (z/zr)^alpha, with alpha about one seventh (0.143) in neutral conditions over open land and 0.11 over open water

Wikipedia, Roughness length: the terrain table from 0.0002 m for open sea to 2 m or more for a city centre, and the log wind profile in which the speed varies with the logarithm of height over that length

Wikipedia, Log wind profile: the logarithmic profile holds in the lowest 100 m of the boundary layer, is more reliable than the power law below about 20 m, and both agree between 20 m and 100 m in neutral conditions
